parts.display_text: Electrons accelerated from rest through a potential difference have de Broglie wavelength 0.100 nm. The potential difference is quadrupled. Assuming non-relativistic motion, determine the new de Broglie wavelength.

answer.text: The kinetic energy eV quadruples, so p = √(2meV) doubles. From λ = h/p, the wavelength halves to 0.0500 nm.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q9:whole.hint: Ask which observation each model can explain, rather than assuming one model explains every experiment.
notes: Interference and diffraction show wave behaviour; the photoelectric effect shows quantized energy transfer. Use the model suited to the observation.
Wave–particle duality does not mean every classical wave property and every classical particle property are observed simultaneously in one measurement.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q37:whole.hint: Consider the energy carried by one photon and the energy needed to release one electron.
notes: Einstein’s photoelectric equation is hf = φ + E_k,max. At threshold, hf₀ = φ; a stopping potential gives E_k,max = eV_stop.

Above threshold, intensity mainly changes the number of emitted electrons; frequency changes the maximum kinetic energy. Below threshold, greater intensity cannot compensate for insufficient photon energy.

sup-064316255265a882-0HL1q39:whole.hint: Connect the particle’s wavelength to its momentum, rather than treating it as a photon.
notes: The de Broglie wavelength is λ = h/p. For a non-relativistic particle, p = mv or √(2mE_k).

If accelerated from rest through a voltage magnitude V, E_k = |q|V. Use this only in the non-relativistic regime; E = hc/λ is a photon relation, not a general massive-particle kinetic-energy equation.
